title: Welcome to my Digital Garden
text:
There are two large sections; Rough Notes and Refined Notes.
The Rough Notes folder will contain first draft notes/rough work just to be able to organize everything later. These will be messy so be warned.
The Refined Notes folder will contain pages that are fully organized, with links between pages so that it’s easier to see connections and also refer back to any theorems/results. If you’re not sure where to start, I recommend starting here and look at some of the “Navigation pages” listed there.
The Resources page is just a list of math-related resources that I want to store. I may not have necessarily read all of them, nor have I necessarily used them to create this wiki. Feel free to take a look at those for your next math read!

title: Welcome to my Digital Garden
text:
About me
Hello! I go by M, I recently graduated with a BSc in Pure Math, and I hope to go to graduate school to eventually become a professor in an Algebra-related field.
I decided to build this math wiki (of sorts) so I can prepare myself for a Master’s while I take a break from school to save up some money. The biggest struggle I had in undergraduate was how interconnected mathematics is, and I needed a big wiki for myself so I could see these connections + for organization purposes, but never had the time. I’m hoping this wiki is of use for others on their mathematical journey! I’ll be adding to this wiki constantly so stay tuned :))
Feel free to contact me via any of the following;

email: msarchives314@gmail.com
Instagram: @msarchives314
X: @ms_archives314

Disclaimers and Regulation

I am open to constructive feedback! If you find any of the following please feel free to contact me and I will edit the wiki to the best of my ability;

Errors - not everything is 100% accurate
Inconsistencies in analogies, interpretations, generalizations - a lot of those will be personal so there may be caveats or might just not work at all
Poor formatting/layout - if pages feel disorganized please tell me how you would like to see it improved

Do not claim this work as your own - I have put a lot of time and effort into creating this, examples of this include but are not limited to;

Academic dishonesty - using proofs or answers to examples or other in assignments, papers, etc

This resembles a blog more than anything! Please don’t use this as a citation unless you are given permission or you think it is appropriate

Number Systems - An introduction to the sets of numbers.
Logical Operators - An introduction to logical operator notations and truth tables.
Basic Set Theory - This is where we define the idea of sets and establish notation pertaining to them.
Proof Techniques - A list of commonly used proof techniques.
Functions - An introduction to functions (or maps may be used interchangeably).

In some branches of math, we tend to focus on one or some of these sets of numbers, or some [[Basic Set Theory#^def-cartesian-product|Cartesian product]] of these sets.






TipDefinition 0.1 - Integers



The set of “integers” is the set, \(\Z:=\set{0,\pm1,\pm2,\ldots}\). The Z stands for the German word for numbers, “Zahlen”.








TipDefinition 0.2 - Natural Numbers



The “natural numbers” is the set of positive [[Number Systems#^def-integers|integers]] and \(0\), \(\N:=\set{x\in\Z\mid x\geq0}\).


Related: Number Theory >
Related: Group Theory >






TipDefinition 0.3 - Rationals



The set of “rationals” is \[
\Q:=\set{\frac{a}{b}\middle| a,b\in\Z}
\]


Related: Ring Theory >






TipDefinition 0.4 - Real Numbers



We define the set of “real numbers”, or “reals”, as \[
\R:=\set{\text{all decimal expansions}}
\]


Related: Analysis >






TipDefinition 0.5 - Complex Numbers



The set of “complex numbers” is denoted by \[
\C:=\set{a+bi\mid a,b\in\R, i^2=-1}
\]


Related: Complex Analysis >






TipNotation 0.1



To denote strictly positive elements of a set of numbers, we’ll use a plus sign on the top right of the set symbol. e.g. \(\Z^+,\Q^+,\R^+\).

title: Logical Operators
text:
CautionPrerequisites






None










TipDefinition 0.1 - Statement



A “statement” is a sentence which can be classified as either true or false, which we will abbreviate with T and F.








TipNotation 0.1 - Logical operators



Let \(p, q\) each be statements.

\(\neg p\) – not \(p\), “negation” of \(p\)
\(p\land q\) – \(p\) “and” \(q\)
\(p\lor q\) – \(p\) “or” \(q\)
\(p\implies q\) – \(p\) “implies” \(q\)
\(p\iff q\) – \(p\) “if and only if” \(q\), meaning \(p\implies q\) and \(p\impliedby q\)









TipDefinition 0.2 - Truth Table



A “truth table” is a table that lists whether a statements with a logical operator yields T or F.








WarningExample 0.1



The above definition of truth table is left vague on purpose, since it’s easier to show an example rather than describing it. Let \(p,q\) be statements. Consider the following table;

where the first two columns are given. What will the next statements yield for each combination of \(p\) and \(q\)?








ImportantAnswer





For \(\neg p\), we yield the opposite of \(p\), meaning if \(p\) is T then \(\neg p\) is F and vice versa. The analog is true for \(\neg q\).
\(p\land q\) is T only when both of \(p\) and \(q\) are T, otherwise it is F. > \(p\lor q\) is F only when both of \(p\) and \(q\) are F, otherwise it is T.
\(p\implies q\) is trickier. First the statement itself is saying “if \(p\) is T, then \(q\) is T”. So if both are T, then this statement is also T. If \(p\) is T and \(q\) is F, this statement is not satisfied, thus it is F. If \(p\) is F and \(q\) is T, we still yield T, since there is no information saying otherwise. If both are F, then similarly, we yield T, since this is still possible.
\(p\iff q\) requires that the symbol for both sides must match each other.

TipDefinition 0.3 - Tautology and Contradiction



If a statement is always true, then that statement is a “tautology”.
If a statement is always false, then that statement is a “contradiction”.








TipDefinition 0.4 - Converse, Inverse, Contrapositive




The “converse” of \(p\implies q\) is \(q\implies p\)
The “inverse” of \(p\implies q\) is \((\neg p)\implies (\neg q)\)
The “contrapositive” of \(p\implies q\) is \((\neg q)\implies (\neg p)\)

title: Basic Set Theory
text:
CautionPrerequisites






Logical Operators










TipDefinition 0.1 - Sets



A collection of mathematical objects is called a “set”, usually denoted with a capital letter. An object in a set is called an “element” or “member” of that set.








TipNotation 0.1



Set notation works as follows. There will be curly brackets with either a list of elements or conditions which dictate the objects which will be contained. For example, \[
\begin{align}
A&=\set{a,b,c,\ldots}\\
B&=\set{x\mid\text{condition}}
\end{align}
\] where the \(|\) is read as “such that”.
Other common symbols that will appear are \(\in,\cup,\cap\), read as “in”, “union”, and “intersection” respectively.








TipDefinition 0.2 - Union and Intersection



Union is defined as follows; \[
A\cup B:=\set{a\in A\text{ or }b\in B}
\]
Intersection is defined as follows; \[
A\cap B:=\set{a\in A\mid a\in B}
\]








TipDefinition 0.3 - Subsets



Let \(S,T\) be sets. \(S\) is a “subset” of \(T\) if all elements in \(S\) are also contained in \(T\). \(S\) is a “proper subset” if we also have that \(S\neq T\).








TipNotation 0.2



If \(S\) is a subset of \(T\), we can write \(S\subseteq T\) or \(T\supseteq S\) depending on the context. If \(S\) is a proper subset of \(T\), we write \(S\subset T\) or \(T\supset S\).








WarningExample 0.1 - Some sets of numbers are subsets of another



We can describe our common sets of numbers to be related by being subsets; \[
\Z^+\subseteq\N\subseteq\Z\subseteq\Q\subseteq\R\subseteq\C
\] Of course there is more to relate but this suffices for the majority of studies of mathematics in my opinion.








NoteRemark 0.1



Notice how the wording of the definition for subsets also allows for one to state that for any set \(S\), we can say \(S\subseteq S\).








TipDefinition 0.4 - Empty set



In some cases, we want to define a set such that it has no elements. We call this the “empty set” or the “null set”. This tends to be useful in probability.








TipNotation 0.3



We denote the empty set with \(\emptyset\)








WarningExample 0.3 - Empty set by Intersection



We can construct the following set; \[
A=\set{x\in\R\mid x<0\text{ and }x>0}
\] and we see that this is not possible since the two conditions would contradict each other due to the definition of \(<\) and \(>\), therefore \(A=\emptyset\). A more technical way to justify this would be because we have a “total ordering” in the real numbers. Next consider \[
B=\set{x\in\R^+\middle|\frac{2x}{x+1}>1\text{ and }x<\frac{1}{2}}
\]
This will also end up yielding the empty set. We rearrange the first condition as follows; \[
\begin{align*}
  \frac{2x}{x+1}&>1 \\
   2x&>x+1 \\
   x&>1
\end{align*}
\] which we then notice that \(x>1>\frac{1}{2}\) which again is a contradiction to the second condition. Hence \(B=\emptyset\).








TipDefinition 0.5 - Order/Cardinality



Under this context, order and cardinality mean the same thing; the number of elements in a set, \(A\). The word “order” is used in many different contexts to have slightly different - but still equivalent meaning. Under the context of set theory, we’ll use cardinality to avoid confusion.








TipNotation 0.4



The cardinality of the set \(A\) is denoted by \(\abs{A}\)








TipTechnique 0.1 - Double Inclusion



Let \(S, S'\) be sets that are defined differently. Sometimes it is in our interest to prove that \(S=S'\), despite having arose from separate contexts. In this case, we often prove that \(S\subseteq S'\) and \(S\supseteq S'\) by showing that an arbitrary element in the subset will always be contained in the subset. This implies equality because this characteristic is unique to equal sets, due to the definition of subset. We call this proof method “double inclusion”.








WarningExample 0.4 - Using double inclusion



Let \(S:=\set{x\in\R\mid1\leq x\leq2}, T:=\set{5x\mid x\in S}\).
Claim to be shown; \(T=\set{y\in\R\mid5\leq y\leq10}\).








ImportantAnswer





We use double inclusion to show this.
(\(\subseteq\))
Suppose \(t\in T\implies t=5x\) for some \(x\in S\). By algebra, we know that \(1\leq x\leq 2\implies 5\leq5x=t\leq10\) which by definition means that \(t\in\set{y\in\R\mid 5\leq y\leq 10}\) as needed.
(\(\supseteq\)) Suppose \(5z\in\set{y\in\R\mid 5\leq y\leq10}\) for some \(z\in\R\), \(\implies5\leq 5z\leq10\) by definition. Then \(1\leq z\leq 2\) by algebra \(\implies z\in S\). Therefore, by definition of \(T\), we see that \(5z\in T\) as required.
\(\therefore T=\set{y\in\R\mid 5\leq y\leq10}\) by double inclusion.









TipDefinition 0.6 - Ordered pair



An ordered pair is a mathematical object with two entries, the first and second, written as \((x,y)\), where the order of the two entries will yield different results. e.g. \((4,5)\neq(5,4)\). A use case of this is coordinates on the Euclidean plane.








TipDefinition 0.7 - Cartesian Product



The “Cartesian product” of two sets \(A,B\) is the set of all ordered pairs with the first entry as an element of \(A\) and the second an element of \(B\).








TipNotation 0.5



Cartesian product is denoted as follows; \[
A\times B:=\set{(a,b)\mid a\in A, b\in B}
\]

title: Proof Techniques
text:
CautionPrerequisites






Logical Operators
Basic Set Theory










TipDefinition 0.1 - Types of results and miscellaneous terminology




“Theorem” - An important mathematical result, usually the punchline
“Proposition”/“Lemma” - A less important result, but is necessary in the proof of a bigger theorem
“Corollary” - A somewhat straightforward consequence from a previous result
“Remark” - May be similar to a corollary, or a note about language used
“Technique” - A generalized strategy in order to solve a problem/prove a result
“Algorithm” - A generalized step-by-step to perform some sort of computation
“Definition” - A word, phrase, variable, or other which we define
“Axiom” - Usually a rule which we define to create some space with a sort of ‘order’
“Assume” - A condition which we take for granted for the proof
“Arbitrary” - Any mathematical object (within some set of conditions)
“Consider”/“Let” - Signalling that we are using a constant (may be explicit or arbitrary) or some fixed mathematical object
“WTS” - Short for “want to show”, makes the goal clearer









NoteRemark 0.1



Note that most, if not all, mathematical statements can be read as \(p\implies q\) to some capacity, where \(p\) is some condition and \(q\) is the result we wish to prove.


For all of the following techniques, consider we have the statement \(p\implies q\) which we wish to prove, unless stated otherwise.






TipTechnique 0.1 - Direct Proof



A “direct proof” is when we start by assuming \(p\) is true, then by logic, definitions, axioms, and/or previous results, we make our way to getting the statement \(q\).








TipTechnique 0.2 - Proof by Contrapositive



“Proof by contrapositive” is when we show the contrapositive of the statement is true, that is \((\neg q) \implies (\neg p)\), since this statement is logically equivalent to \(p\implies q\), as shown in Logical Operators - Example 0.2.








TipTechnique 0.3 - Proof by Contradiction



Sometimes none of the above techniques are clear answers to prove a statement, so we instead use “proof by contradiction”. This is when we assume that \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false. This should eventually lead to some sort of absurdity/contradiction.








TipTechnique 0.4 - Cases



A “proof by cases” is when we must divide the conditions into separate cases which still satisfy \(p\), and then use the appropriate proof technique on each case. In order to have a proof by cases, one must be careful of how each case is constructed, as the union must cover the whole set which the result is built upon, as well as not intersect.








TipTechnique 0.5 - Principle of Mathematical Induction



If we are to prove a statement for all integers larger than some \(n_0\in\Z\), in the case of a regular direct proof, we would show that \(p\implies q\) for an arbitrary \(n\), which then by the arbitrariness of \(n\) would suffice. However, this does not necessarily work for all proofs, so we instead employ the “principle of mathematical induction”.
Let \(S(n)\) be the statement \(p\implies q\) using the integer \(n\). The idea of this proof technique is to use the \(n\)th case to prove the \(n+1\)th case, which effectively proves the case for all integers larger than \(n_0\).
The steps are as follows;
(i) Prove the “base case” - show that \(S(n_0)\) is true
(ii) Inductive step - assume \(S(n)\) is true for some \(n\geq n_0\), show that \(S(n+1)\) is true using the assumption
Once these steps are satisfied, then by the principle of mathematical induction (PMI), \(S(n)\) is true for all integers \(n\geq n_0\).








TipRemark 0.2



One can imagine PMI to be the same as lining up infinite dominos; if the first domino falls (base case is true), then the next domino will fall, and so forth, and the \(n\)th domino falls which causes the \(n+1\)th domino to fall (inductive step).


The proof that PMI works is due to the property of the integers.
Related: Number Theory >






TipTechnique 0.6 - Principle of Strong Induction



Let \(n_0\in\Z\) and \(S(n)\) is a statement for the integer \(n\geq n_0\).
(i) Prove the “base case” - show that \(S(n_0)\) is true
(ii) Inductive step - assume \(S(n_0), S(n_0+1),\ldots, S(n)\) are all true for some \(n\geq n_0\), show that \(S(n+1)\) is true using the assumption
This is what we call the “principle of strong induction”. This method is different from PMI above as we have a different amount of information which we can make use of in the inductive step.








ImportantProof





The proof for the principle of strong induction is by ordinary induction on \(n\).
Let us rephrase the goal in a way which matches the definition of induction. Let \(P(n)\) be the statement that \(S(k)\) is true for all \(n_0\leq k\leq n\). We will use induction on \(n\) to show that \(P(n)\) is true for all \(n\geq n_0\). Moreover, our statement to be proven is “steps (i) and (ii) are true implies \(S(n)\) is true \(\forall n\geq n_0\)”.
(Base case: \(P(n_0)\))
\(P(n_0)\) is the statement \(S(n_0)\) is true. This is provided by the assumption that step (i) is true.
(Inductive step: Assume \(P(n)\) is true for some \(n\geq n_0\), WTS \(P(n+1)\) is true)
\(P(n)\) means \(S(k)\) is true for all \(n_0\leq k\leq n\). Since we assume step (ii) is true, this implies that \(S(n+1)\) is also true. Combining the two statements gives us that \(S(k)\) is true for all \(n_0\leq k\leq n+1\), i.e. \(P(n+1)\) is true as required.
Therefore, by PMI, \(P(n)\) is true for all \(n\geq n_0\). Hence, the principle of strong induction works for any statement, due to the arbitrariness of \(S(k)\).
